reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function mutations in TNFRSF11B, the gene encoding osteoprotegerin
Loss of osteoprotegerin removes inhibition of the RANK-RANKL pathway, driving grossly accelerated bone turnover throughout the skeleton
Presents in infancy or early childhood with bone pain, fractures, progressive long-bone bowing, and enlargement and deformity of the skull
Markedly elevated serum alkaline phosphatase and other bone turnover markers reflect the very high remodelling rate
Progressive deafness is common, and skull expansion can raise concern for cranial nerve compromise
Unlike classic adult Paget disease it is generalised rather than focal and manifests in childhood
Antiresorptive therapy with bisphosphonates can suppress the excessive turnover and improve symptoms and deformity
reference.pathophysiology: Juvenile Paget disease is caused by biallelic inactivating mutations in TNFRSF11B, which encodes osteoprotegerin, a decoy receptor that normally binds RANKL and prevents it from activating RANK on osteoclast precursors. Without functional osteoprotegerin, RANKL signalling is unopposed, leading to greatly increased osteoclast formation and activity. Coupled to this is a compensatory surge in osteoblastic bone formation, so the skeleton undergoes extremely rapid but disorganised remodelling. The resulting woven, mechanically weak bone produces widespread deformity, bowing, fractures, and skull enlargement, and the very high turnover is mirrored by strikingly raised alkaline phosphatase.
additionalDifferentials: Other high-turnover metabolic bone disorders of childhood
additionalInvestigations: Serum alkaline phosphatase and additional bone turnover markers
Serum calcium, phosphate, and vitamin D to characterise mineral status
Plain radiographs showing generalised osteopenia or sclerosis, bowing, and skull thickening
Cranial imaging when skull-base involvement or neurological features are present
redFlags: Progressive hearing loss or cranial neuropathy from skull involvement
Recurrent fractures and rapidly worsening bony deformity
Signs of raised intracranial pressure from skull expansion
Retinal or vascular calcification and cardiovascular complications reported in some forms
reference.prognosis: Untreated disease causes progressive deforming bone disease, fractures, and deafness with substantial disability, but antiresorptive therapy can markedly reduce turnover and improve the clinical course, making early diagnosis important.
pitfalls: Confusing the generalised childhood disease with focal adult Paget disease
Overlooking early hearing loss that warrants audiological follow-up
Attributing the very high alkaline phosphatase to liver disease rather than bone turnover
Delaying antiresorptive treatment that can alter the disease trajectory
references: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
GeneReviews / peer-reviewed reviews of juvenile Paget disease (idiopathic hyperphosphatasia)
management: Suppress the grossly accelerated bone turnover with antiresorptive bisphosphonate therapy as the mainstay of treatment
Ensure adequate calcium and vitamin D repletion to support mineralisation during antiresorptive therapy
Monitor treatment response with serial alkaline phosphatase and other bone turnover markers
Provide orthopaedic management of fractures, long-bone bowing and deformity
Undertake audiological assessment and provide hearing aids for progressive deafness
Perform cranial and skull-base surveillance for nerve compromise from skull expansion
Offer physiotherapy and mobility support to preserve function
Arrange autosomal recessive genetic counselling and family screening
